name: Laughlin on Coherence Limits
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: A Nobel Physicist's Case Against the Hype
lesson.summary: Robert Laughlin, who won a Nobel Prize for work in condensed matter physics, has been one of the more prominent scientific skeptics of quantum computing, arguing from decades of lab experience that large scale quantum coherence may be far harder to achieve than roadmaps assume.
lesson.body:
Robert Laughlin shared the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining the fractional quantum Hall effect, a result that came out of exactly the kind of delicate, low temperature, many particle quantum experiments that quantum computing now depends on. That background matters, because his skepticism about quantum computing is not the skepticism of an outsider who does not understand the field. It is the skepticism of someone who has spent a career watching how quantum effects behave, and misbehave, in real materials. The details of his specific public arguments have appeared in various talks, essays, and interviews over the years, and this chapter will not pretend to quote him precisely or cite a specific paper, but the general shape of his position is well known in the physics community and worth taking seriously.

The core of the argument connects directly to the decoherence problem covered earlier. Decoherence is often described in quantum computing marketing as an engineering obstacle, something like vibration in a telescope or noise in a radio signal, which can in principle be filtered out or engineered around with enough clever design and enough money. Laughlin's line of skepticism, built from condensed matter intuition, treats decoherence as something closer to a law of nature: the tendency of a complicated quantum system to entangle with its environment is not a nuisance sitting on top of otherwise clean physics, it is close to the default behavior of any large, warm, or imperfectly isolated system. Keeping dozens or hundreds of qubits coherent long enough to do useful work is not simply a matter of scaling up a technique that already works for a handful of qubits.

This distinction matters enormously for how a student should read quantum computing roadmaps. A roadmap that says "we improved coherence times by a factor of ten this year, so a hundredfold improvement is a few years away" is implicitly assuming that the difficulty scales in a predictable, engineerable way, similar to how transistor density improved during the decades of Moore's Law. A skeptic in Laughlin's mold would push back hard on that analogy. Transistors are classical objects that do not care about being observed or entangled with their surroundings. Qubits do. There is no guaranteed law that says coherence at scale gets easier just because coherence at small scale got a little better.

None of this proves that large scale, fault tolerant quantum computing is impossible. Laughlin's skepticism is a hypothesis grounded in physical intuition and experience, not a mathematical proof of a hard limit, and serious experimental progress on error correction has continued since these kinds of arguments were first raised. The honest position is that nobody, including Laughlin, can currently prove with certainty how far coherence engineering can be pushed.

What a credentialed skeptic like this offers a student is not a verdict but a useful counterweight. When every recruiting brochure and funding announcement describes decoherence as a solved in principle problem awaiting more engineering effort, it is worth remembering that at least one Nobel laureate with direct experience in this exact kind of physics was not convinced that framing was right. Holding both the optimistic roadmap and the skeptical counterargument in mind at the same time, without collapsing to either extreme, is the actual skill this book is trying to teach.
